forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, ℓ with 0 ≤ k, ℓ ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose ℓ]_q is a polynomial in q, then it has only nonnegative coefficients.

forbidden_claims.label: lem_20260329092547_6a64d34a
forbidden_claims.statement_nl: For integers a, b, r with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0, let q be an indeterminate, define (q;q)_n := product_{j=1}^n (1 - q^j) for n >= 0 with (q;q)_0 := 1, set R_{a,b,r}(q) := ((q;q)_{r+b} (q;q)_a) / ((q;q)_{r+a} (q;q)_b), and define D := r (b - a). Assume that R_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Then for every integer j with 0 <= j <= floor(D/2), the coefficient of q^j in R_{a,b,r}(q) is a nonnegative integer.

forbidden_claims.label: lem_20260329074016_d9949d95
forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. Assume that for every positive integer d one has floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d). Then P_{a,b,r}(q) is a polynomial in Z[q], and every coefficient of P_{a,b,r}(q) is nonnegative.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integers a, b, r, j with 0 <= a <= b and r, j nonnegative, let I be the set of integers from a+1 through b and let F be the finite product over i in I of (1 minus q to the power r+i) times the geometric series in q to the power i. Then the coefficient of q to the j in F equals the sum over all pairs (S, lambda) where S is a subset of I and lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I whose element-sum plus the sum of r+s over s in S is j, with each pair weighted by minus one to the power of the size of S.
quantifier_order: For all integers a, b, r, j satisfying 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0 and j >= 0.
Define I as the integers from a+1 through b.
Define F as the finite product over i in I of (1 minus q to the power r+i) times the geometric series sum over m >= 0 of q to the power m i.
Define X_j as the set of pairs (S, lambda) with S a subset of I and lambda a finite multiset of elements of I such that the total sum of lambda plus the sum of r+s over s in S equals j.
Then the coefficient of q to the j in F equals the signed sum over X_j of minus one to the power of the size of S.

payload.statement_nl: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and j >= 0. Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Define the formal power series F_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) * sum_{m>=0} q^(m i)). Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let I = {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. Fix j >= 0. Since a >= 0, every i in I is a positive integer. Hence any term q^(m i) with m > floor(j/i) has degree greater than j, so it cannot contribute to the coefficient of q^j in a product whose other factors also have only nonnegative exponents. Therefore
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = [q^j] product_{i in I} ((1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
The right-hand side is now the coefficient of a finite product of finite sums, so we may expand it by the ordinary distributive law.

For each i in I, write
(1 - q^(r+i)) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i) = (sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)) + (- q^(r+i) sum_{m=0}^{floor(j/i)} q^(m i)).
In the full expansion of the product, choose the second bracket exactly for those i belonging to some subset S of I. For each i, also choose one integer m_i >= 0 from the geometric sum. The resulting monomial is then
(-1)^(|S|) q^( sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S} (r+s) ).
Hence
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all families (m_i)_{i in I} of nonnegative integers satisfying sum_{i in I} m_i i + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
(The bounds m_i <= floor(j/i) are automatic from the displayed equation, so they do not need to be written separately.)

Now such a family (m_i)_{i in I} is the same thing as a finite multiset lambda of elements of I: namely, lambda contains exactly m_i copies of i for each i in I. Conversely, every finite multiset of elements of I gives such a family of multiplicities. Under this bijection,
|lambda| = sum_{i in I} i m_i.
Therefore, for each fixed S, the inner sum is exactly over those finite multisets lambda of elements of I such that
|lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j.
So we get
[q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum over all subsets S of I of sum over all finite multisets lambda of elements of I with |lambda| + sum_{s in S}(r+s) = j of (-1)^(|S|).
By the definition of X_j, this is exactly
sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|).
Thus [q^j] F_{a,b,r}(q) = sum_{(S,lambda) in X_j} (-1)^(|S|), as claimed.

Finally, the sum over X_j is finite: if (S,lambda) belongs to X_j, then |lambda| <= j, and since every element of I is at least 1, lambda has at most j elements. Because I is finite, there are only finitely many such multisets lambda, and there are only finitely many subsets S of I. So the right-hand side is well-defined.
result_payload.proof_summary: For the coefficient of q^j, truncate each geometric series at m <= floor(j/i). Expanding the resulting finite product amounts to choosing a subset S of indices where the factor -q^(r+i) is taken, together with multiplicities m_i from the geometric series. This gives monomials of sign (-1)^(|S|) and degree sum_i m_i i + sum_{s in S}(r+s). Interpreting the multiplicity tuple (m_i) as a finite multiset lambda of I with |lambda| = sum_i i m_i yields exactly the stated signed sum over X_j.
